questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.text: A language of an automaton can have an infinitely long string (or many of them) in it.
A language of an automaton can contain infinitely many strings.
A language of an automaton can contain no strings.
A language of an automaton can contain finitely many strings.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

Detailed Video Explanation: https://youtu.be/wvsijTYqVq0?t=621

  • Languages are sets of strings.
  • Strings are sequences of characters.
  • Characters are individual symbols.
  • Alphabets are sets of characters.
  • A language is a set of strings, a string is a (finite) sequence of characters, and a character is an element of an alphabet.

The language of an automaton is the set of strings that it accepts.

If $D$ is an automaton that processes characters from the alphabet $\Sigma$, then ${L}(\boldsymbol{D})$ is formally defined as
$$
{L}(D)=\left\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid D \text { accepts } w\right\}
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)
Option B, C and D are easy. Let me decscribe why option A is incorrect.

Consider the language $L = \Sigma^*, \Sigma=\{1\}$. Consider the following questions.

Q1 Is there a string in L whose length is greater than 100?
Answer - Yes, take $s =1^{999}$

Q2 Is there a string in L whose length is greater than 1000?
Answer - Yes, take $s =1^{1999}$. Obviously, you are no longer able to take $s =1^{999}$, because its length does have an upper bound, which we have crossed.

Q3 Is there a string in L whose length is greater than 1 billion?
Answer - Yes, take $s = 1^{10^{12}}$. Ofcourse, you are no longer able to use $s = 1^{1999}$.

Now generalize this argument. If person A asks you the question "Is there a string in L whose length is greater than x?". The second person can always answer this question by providing an example string whose length is greater than $x$. But, the person A can always raise $x$ to a value more than the length of string provided as answer to previous question, and ask a new question. This QA session can continue forever. Therefore, if you think sufficiently deeply about it, the length of every string is finite, since an upper bound will always exist on the length of string (the value $x$). However, there is no doubt that the language itself has infinite elements in it. The reason that there are infinite elements is given by the fact that the QA session can continue forever, there is no bound to how many questions person A can ask.

questions.qtext:
Here's the operator precedence for regular expressions, from highest to lowest:
$$
\begin{gathered}
(\text{R}) \\
\text{R}^* \\
\text{R}_1 \text{R}_2 \\
\text{R}_1 \cup \text{R}_2
\end{gathered}
$$

Consider the regular expression
$$ab^*c\cup d$$

How many of the strings below are in the language described by this regular expression?

  • $ababc$
  • $abd$
  • $ac$
  • $abcd$
questions.solution:
Answer: 1

Selected solution (score: 4)

Detailed Video Explanation: https://youtu.be/wvsijTYqVq0?feature=shared&t=4453

Given regular expression $ab^*c\cup d \equiv (ab^*c) + (d)$

Analysis by given strings:

So, the language will be $\{d, ac, abc, abbc, abbbc, ……...\}$

  • $ababc : \color{Red}\text{Not possible}.$
  • $abd : \color{Red}\text{Not possible}.$
  • $ac : \color{Green}\text{Possible}.$
  • $abcd : \color{Red}\text{Not possible}.$

So, Only $1$ string is described by this $RE$.

$\color{Green}{Ans: 1}$

Meaning of these things:

$(R)$ = Regular expression with same meaning as $R$

$R^*$ = Kleene closure of language $R$

$R_{1}R_{2}$ = Concatenation of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$

$R_{1} \cup R_{2}$ = Union of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ which is same as $R_{1} + R_{2}$

questions.qtext:
• Let $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$.
  • Let $\text{L}=\left\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid w\right.$ contains at most one $a \}$.

Which of the following is/are a regular expression for $\text{L}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Selected solution (score: 1)

Detailed Video Explanation: https://youtu.be/wvsijTYqVq0?t=4635

$\sum = \{a,b\}; \; \; L = \{w \in \sum^* | \text{w contains at most one a}\}$

  1. $b^*(a^*\cup\varepsilon)b^*$ : strings generated- $bbaaabbb, baaaaabbb, bbabbb$. Here, $a$ can come any no. of times but we want at most one.
  2. $b^*ab^*\cup b^*$ : strings generated- $bbbabbbbb, babbbbbb, bbbbbbbabbb, bbbabb$. Here, $a$ comes only once. So, it is regular expresssion of $L$
  3. $b^*(a \cup \varepsilon)b^*$ : strings generated- $bbbabbbb,bbabb, bbbbabbb, bbabbbbbb$. Here, $a$ comes only once. So, it is also correct regular expression.
  4. $b^*a^*b^* \cup b^*$ : strings generated- $bbbaaabbbbbbb, bbbaaaabbbbb$. Here, $a$ can come any no. of times but we want at most one.

$\color{Green}Ans: B,C$

questions.qtext:
The state elimination algorithm gives a way to transform a finite automaton (DFA or NFA) into a regular expression. It's a really beautiful algorithm once you get the hang of it, so we thought that we'd let you try it out on a particular example.

In the following Generalized NFA, we want to remove state $q_1:$


If we remove state $q_1,$ then we get two transitions(edges), one from $q_s$ to $q_1$ (this new edge is shown in the figure below) and another from $q_2$ to $q_2.$

What regex should go on this edge?
A. $\text{R}_{12} \text{R}_{21}$
B. $\text{R}_{12} \text{R}_{22} * \text{R}_{21}$
C. $\text{R}_{21} \text{R}_{12}$
D. $\text{R}_{21} \text{R}_{11} * \text{R}_{12}$
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

Detailed Video Explanation: https://youtu.be/1iEubMxkN8c?t=1800

Detailed Video Explanation: https://youtu.be/1iEubMxkN8c?t=1800

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

The correct answer is D.

Explanation:

The problem asks us to find the regular expression for the new transition created from state $q_2$ to itself when state $q_1$ is eliminated.

Here is the step-by-step application of the State Elimination Algorithm:

  1. Identify the Path: We want to find the path that starts at $q_2$, goes through the state being removed ($q_1$), and returns to $q_2$. This creates a new "bypass" self-loop on $q_2$.

  2. Break down the path:

    • Step 1: Leave $q_2$ and go to $q_1$. The label on this edge is $R_{21}$.

    • Step 2: While at $q_1$, we can loop any number of times. The label on the self-loop at $q_1$ is $R_{11}$. So, we can traverse this $R_{11}^*$ times.

    • Step 3: Leave $q_1$ and go back to $q_2$. The label on this edge is $R_{12}$.

  3. Concatenate the parts:

    To get the full regex for this specific path, we concatenate the expressions in order:

    $$Path = (\text{Edge } q_2 \to q_1) \cdot (\text{Loop at } q_1)^* \cdot (\text{Edge } q_1 \to q_2)$$

    $$Path = R_{21} \cdot R_{11}^* \cdot R_{12}$$

This matches Option D.
